article_title: From through-course summative to adaptive through-year models for large-scale assessment: A literature review
citation: Garron Gianopulos. (2019). From Through-Course Summative to Adaptive Through-Year Models for Large-scale Assessment: A Literature Review. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Match the score aggregation method to a proven model of how students learn the tested material
description: This principle, drawn from Wise's recommendations quoted in the review, holds that methods for combining through-course scores into end-of-year proficiency estimates must rest on validated models of student learning. Wise states that "Methods used for aggregating results from through-course assessments to estimate end of- year proficiency or annual growth should be based on proven models of how students learn the material that is being tested." Otherwise, mid-year results can misestimate end-of-year status and growth.
requirements: Research demonstrating relationships between time of instruction and student mastery of targeted knowledge and skills
constraints: Mid-year results can significantly underestimate or overestimate end-of-year status and growth if the aggregation method is inconsistent with how students actually learn
target_learners: K-12 students assessed through through-year accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of end-of-year proficiency and annual growth from interim scores
examples: Wise's End-of-Unit Model uses simple addition when learning is bounded to each period; his Continuous Learning Model uses projection-based weighted averages when learning is continuous

article_title: Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named
citation: Nama, R. (2026). Agentic Literacy Debt: A Structural Problem the AI Literacy Field Has Not Yet Named. Author's accepted manuscript, AI and Ethics (Springer Nature). https://arxiv.org/
title: Agentic literacy debt: a compounding societal deficit from deploying agentic AI without literacy infrastructure
description: The paper defines agentic literacy debt as the accumulating deficit that grows "when agentic AI systems are deployed at scale without the literacy infrastructure users need to govern them." Borrowed from technical debt, it compounds through three reinforcing channels: normalization of opaque delegation (a ratchet effect of inherited, rarely revoked permission grants), multi-agent ecosystem complexity, and institutional path dependence. It extends Ladson-Billings' education debt and Petrozzino's ethical debt to systems that act autonomously on citizens' behalf.
requirements: Deployment of autonomous agents without frameworks enabling users to understand, supervise, and contest their actions is what adds to the debt.
constraints: Unlike ethical debt, incurred at design, it is incurred at the point of deployment and compounds with every user interaction without adequate literacy infrastructure.
target_learners: users, patients, consumers, and citizens on whose behalf agents act
target_learning_goals: governing autonomous AI agents: understanding, supervising, and contesting agent actions
examples: The author cites OpenClaw walletdrain attacks and the EchoLeak vulnerability as visible consequences of the gap.

article_title: Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning
citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Agentic AI systems defined by three behavioural traits: autonomy, proactivity, and reactivity
description: The article defines agentic systems as digital actors with three core behavioural traits: "autonomy to function without continuous human intervention, proactiveness to initiate goal-directed actions, and reactiveness to adapt to changing contexts". Unlike conventional dialogue systems, proactive AI agents can anticipate outcomes, take initiative, and strategically plan. A key functional advantage is the ability to use external tools (databases, APIs, microservices) while leveraging persistent memory across sessions and communicating across multi-agent networks. The article uses this framework to analyse how such systems interact with established pedagogical principles.
requirements: Persistent memory and access to external tools such as databases, APIs, and microservices to maintain continuity and act across the digital ecosystem
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual lens from the agentic AI literature, not empirically tested in educational settings in this article
target_learners: learners using AI-supported educational applications
target_learning_goals: personalised and real-time adaptive learning

citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Isanka Wijerathne, and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Agentic AI and Pedagogical Best Practice: The Tension Between Automation and Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04543
title: Pedagogically Informed Agentic AI Implementation Matrix mapping six principles to agent actions and friction/fading strategies
description: Table 1 of the article operationalises six pedagogical principles into an actionable design framework, mapping each principle to a specific agent action, a friction or fading strategy, and a learning example. For example, for problem-based learning the agent generates an interactive simulation of a local real-world issue and "refuses to provide a direct 'solution pathway' when stuck, offering clues about where to look instead". The matrix is intended to bridge theory, system architecture, and practice, demonstrating how intentional instructional friction and dynamic scaffolding fading can be embedded across diverse learning contexts.

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Agent-based architectures coordinate intelligence and adaptivity at runtime through modular specialization
description: The chapter presents agent-based architectures as a coordination mechanism for combining LLM intelligence and RL adaptivity within a single system. A multi-agent system distributes instructional responsibility across specialized components—a learner modeling agent, a pedagogical policy agent, a content generation agent, and a safety validation agent—that "can be developed, tested, validated, and updated independently." This extends Phase IV's separation of concerns to intelligent, learned components, enabling runtime coordination where one agent continuously updates a rich learner model while another makes rapid instructional decisions within timescales compatible with interactive gameplay.
requirements: Each agent must have a well-defined interface specifying what information it receives and what it produces
Practical implementations require asynchronous pipelines, with content generation occurring in the background and instructional responses delivered at natural transition points
constraints: Agent-based architectures "remain largely aspirational in fully integrated form" in the current state of the field

Coordination overhead: LLM-based content generation typically requires 500 milliseconds to two seconds, and total multi-agent pipeline response times may exceed what is compatible with moment-to-moment immersive game interaction
Emergent behaviors arising from agent interactions may be harmful and require evaluation methodologies beyond traditional software testing
Transparency and instructor trust require deliberate architectural investment in logging, explanation, and instructor control mechanisms
Validation must assess the decision-making process rather than fixed content, requiring simulation-based evaluation, expert monitoring, and ongoing auditing that does not end at deployment
target_learners: Learners in serious games and immersive simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: Integrated instructional intelligence and real-time adaptivity within unified architectures
examples: Configurations range from a two-agent design pairing learner modeling with policy components to architectures coordinating scenario generation, affective state monitoring, dialogue management, and safety validation simultaneously

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: Agentic software engineering as a discipline: humans frame, specify and judge; agents execute
description: The article's opening conceptual move is that agentic software engineering is a discipline rather than a tool skill: it has principles, named artefacts, recognised failure modes and standards. Its central division of labour is that "humans frame, specify and judge, and agents execute, which means that the human's job is to equip the agent and to verify what it produces." The article names three collapse modes (hand-editing output and losing the audit trail, delegating judgment along with execution, delegating framing itself) and four structural risks: skill atrophy, code opacity, diffuse accountability, and models reproducing training-corpus assumptions.
requirements: Practitioners must be trained to expect the four structural risks and to maintain the division of labour, since none of the risks disappear with experience
constraints: The article states the division of labour is straightforward to state but difficult to maintain in practice, and collapses in predictable ways when violated
target_learners: undergraduate software engineering students
practising developers transitioning to agent-mediated work
target_learning_goals: understanding the human role in agent-directed development
recognising discipline failure modes and structural risks
examples: The curriculum teaches the ACE side of Hassan and colleagues' SASE workbench split while developing enough AEE understanding to direct and verify agent output

citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662
title: Three-theme account of selective engagement with multi-representational visualization tools: agency, representational fit, and legitimacy
description: An explanatory account of why learners engage with or resist available visual scaffolds, constructed inductively through reflexive thematic analysis of interviews and think-alouds. The article reports that "three themes were constructed that characterized variation across participants": agency (students' relationship to cognitive effort and control), representational fit (individual differences in what felt helpful versus overwhelming), and legitimacy (concerns about what tool use signaled about academic identity). article_title: AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation
citation: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361
title: AgenticMath four-stage multi-agent data generation framework
description: AgenticMath is an automated multi-agent framework enforcing quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation. It proceeds in four stages: seed problem filtering (LLM scoring on complexity, information value, and clarity with k-NN score curation), agentic problem generation (rephrase, review, and revise agents with an iterative loop), solution generation (one-shot chain-of-thought prompting), and synthetic-data evaluation with ranking-based selection. The article describes it as "an automated multi-agent framework that enforces quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation," following a "Less Is More" principle to yield a data-efficient, high-quality dataset.
requirements: LLM agents (GPT-4o-mini) for scoring, rephrasing, review, revision, and solution generation
Seed problems sourced from human-authored corpora (GSM8K and MATH)
Quality thresholds: seed filtering score of 3 and review-revise threshold of 4.5 with up to three iterations
constraints: The article notes current study focuses on text-based mathematical problems; multimodal extension remains future work
Scalability under substantially larger data budgets was not evaluated due to computational and resource constraints
target_learners: 3B-8B parameter large language models undergoing supervised fine-tuning
target_learning_goals: Generating high-quality mathematical question-answer pairs to improve LLM mathematical reasoning
examples: Each filtered seed problem is expanded into six rephrased variants; the review-revise loop runs at most three iterations with early stopping once the 4.5 threshold is met

citation: Luis Marquez-Carpintero, Alberto Lopez-Sellers, Miguel Cazorla. (2025). Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06078
title: Agent4Edu: a personalized learning simulator with LLM-based generative agents and a three-operation memory module
description: Agent4Edu is a personalized learning simulator in which "LLM-based generative agents simulate student response data and detailed problem-solving behaviour". Agents carry predefined student profiles, memory modules, and action modules for personalized learning scenarios, selecting, understanding, analyzing, and responding to exercises in a human-like manner. Its memory management system includes three operations: memory retrieval from short- and long-term stores, memory writing that promotes reinforced observations into short- or long-term memory, and memory reflection (summary and corrective forms) occurring exclusively in long-term memory. article_title: The agency gap in AI-supported writing: how reactive and proactive agent designs shape multimodal reasoning
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Kaixun Yang, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2025). The Agency Gap in AI-Supported Writing: How Reactive and Proactive Agent Designs Shape Multimodal Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04398
title: The agency gap: a relational construct describing mismatch between AI agent initiative and learner GenAI literacy
description: The agency gap is the article's primary theoretical contribution: a relational conceptualisation of a mismatch between the initiative an AI agent demands (reactive or proactive) and the learner's capacity to initiate, monitor, evaluate, and internalise AI-supported reasoning. It concerns alignment of learner capability and interaction design rather than an individual deficit. Under-support arises when lower-literacy learners meet strongly reactive environments; over-direction arises when capable learners meet rigidly proactive environments. It is examined through converging evidence from discourse networks, writing outcomes, and reflections, not measured as a latent construct.
requirements: Requires characterising both the agent's initiative structure and the learner's GenAI literacy to diagnose alignment
constraints: The article states it is not a new general theory of agency and not an established or directly measured latent construct; neither agent design is assumed universally superior
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI for academic writing
target_learning_goals: independent multimodal analytical writing
learner agency in human–AI interaction

article_title: Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813
title: Agentivism: a mid-range learning theory of durable human capability through selective delegation, verification, reconstruction, and transfer under reduced support
description: Agentivism is a mid-range conceptual learning theory for human-AI interaction. It defines learning as "durable growth in human capability that occurs when learners delegate selectively to generative or agentic AI, monitor and verify AI contributions, and reconstruct AI-assisted performance into knowledge and skill that remain available beyond the immediate interaction". Its explanatory core lies in "four linked mechanisms (Fig. 1): delegated agency, epistemic monitoring and verification, reconstructive internalization, and transfer under reduced support". The theory treats allocation of agency during interaction as a central explanatory variable and distinguishes assisted performance from learning, arguing that learning can no longer be inferred from performance alone when AI contributes directly to task completion.
requirements: Learning must be judged by what the learner can later explain, adapt, and transfer with reduced dependence on the same AI support, not by immediate task success.
constraints: The article states it "does not claim that all forms of learning through human-AI interaction follow one fixed sequence or can be reduced to a single explanatory principle".
It is not yet a formal computational model of learning and will require refinement as forms of AI support and institutional uses evolve.
target_learners: Learners using generative or agentic AI in writing, inquiry, problem solving, tutoring, and professional learning
target_learning_goals: Durable, transferable human capability developed through human-AI interaction
examples: The article maps six empirically testable propositions (P1–P6) onto the four core mechanisms, illustrating how predictions about learning outcomes arise from specific process components.
key_sources: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813

article_title: A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities
citation: Wang, N., Zou, D., Xie, H., & Qin, S. J. (2026). A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities, and insights from the frontier agent paradigm, exemplified by OpenClaw. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100653
title: Definition of generative AI-powered agentic AI via three core characteristics: task autonomy, goal-directed reasoning, and memory- and context-aware interaction
description: The review defines agentic AI as systems "powered by generative AI, that exhibit goal-directed autonomy": perceiving the environment, reasoning about goals, formulating and executing multi-step plans, adapting behaviour, and coordinating with tools, other agents, or human stakeholders. Three core characteristics distinguish educational agentic systems from general-purpose text generators: task autonomy, goal-directed reasoning and adaptive decision-making, and memory- and context-aware interaction; multi-step planning and multi-agent collaboration may be present but are not required for inclusion.
requirements: A study qualifies when the system is designed for an educational purpose and demonstrates at least one core agentic characteristic; fully autonomous operation is not required, as capability is treated as a matter of degree.
constraints: Studies where generative AI is used only as a general-purpose text-generation or prompt-response tool without a designed educational agent workflow are excluded.
target_learners: Educational AI researchers and system designers
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing agentic educational systems from general-purpose generative AI tools
examples: Concrete examples given include an adaptive tutor diagnosing misconceptions through dialogue, a role-playing simulator adopting a patient or historical persona, a curriculum curator, and multi-agent orchestration under human oversight.

article_title: A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education
citation: Simon Baradziej. (2026). A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education. Social Sciences & Humanities Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2026.103418
title: Defining features of agentic AI: autonomy, planning, tool use, and persistent memory
description: The review defines agentic AI as an architectural class distinguished from generative and rule-based AI by intersecting properties. "Agentic AI denotes a class of system architectures rather than a single technology characterised by several intersecting properties. Autonomy is the foundational attribute: the agent executes tasks and makes decisions without requiring human instruction at each step." Additional properties include reactivity, proactivity, learning ability, tool use, memory, and planning. The review operationalised this definition in screening: a study was classified as agentic when its system met at least three of four criteria (autonomy, planning, tool use, persistent memory).
requirements: Classification as agentic requires meeting at least three of the four defining criteria: autonomy, planning, tool use, and persistent memory
constraints: Generative AI lacks goal-directed planning, tool invocation, and persistent memory as first-class features; traditional autonomous systems execute fixed algorithms without adaptive reasoning
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: distinguishing agentic AI from generative and rule-based AI in educational deployments

article_title: Agentic AI in Education: State of the Art and Future Directions
citation: Kostopoulos, G., Gkamas, V., Rigou, M., & Kotsiantis, S. (2025). Agentic AI in Education: State of the Art and Future Directions. IEEE Access. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3620473
title: Three-axis taxonomy of agentic AI in education: pedagogical role, autonomy level and embodiment
description: The review proposes an organizing taxonomy for educational agentic AI built on three axes. The first axis covers pedagogical roles (tutor, coach/mentor, companion, instructor's assistant, curriculum planner); the second orders systems from reactive to adaptive, proactive and collaborative agents by autonomy; the third distinguishes text-based, graphical/avatar, embodied and multimodal agents. As the authors state, "we propose a taxonomy based on three axes: pedagogical role, autonomy level and embodiment", summarized in their Figure 2.
requirements: Systems are classified by stated purpose, decision-making flexibility and interface modality, so classification requires documented system behavior on each axis
constraints: The taxonomy classifies existing and developing systems as described by the survey; it is a descriptive scheme, not an empirically validated instrument
target_learners: learners across higher education, vocational education and training, and K-12 contexts
target_learning_goals: personalized instruction, self-regulated learning, collaborative problem-solving
examples: The review illustrates autonomy levels with rule-based chatbots as reactive agents and multi-agent systems as collaborative agents engaging in joint planning with users

article_title: Agentic AI in Education: State of the Art and Future Directions
citation: Kostopoulos, G., Gkamas, V., Rigou, M., & Kotsiantis, S. (2025). Agentic AI in Education: State of the Art and Future Directions. IEEE Access. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3620473
title: Six-criterion operational checklist for classifying a system as agentic
description: The review operationalizes agentic AI with a checklist of six verifiable criteria covering autonomy, reasoning, memory, planning, goal-directed interaction and related capabilities. A system counts as agentic if it meets at least four criteria: "In this survey, a system is considered agentic if it satisfies at least four of these criteria." The threshold is intended to exclude reactive chatbots while accommodating diverse architectures; the authors give the example of a tutoring system that plans multi-turn lessons, remembers learner progress, triggers prompts autonomously and provides formative feedback.
requirements: Documented evidence of at least four of the six criteria, reflecting "the minimum combination of autonomy, reasoning, memory, and action required for goal-directed behavior in educational contexts"
constraints: The ≥4-criterion threshold is the authors' own convention for this survey, chosen to balance inclusiveness against classifying reactive chatbots as agentic
target_learners: researchers and designers evaluating educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: consistent identification of agentic capabilities in educational AI systems
examples: A static FAQ bot lacking planning or persistence would not qualify under the checklist, per the review's own contrast example

article_title: ‘Models of’ versus ‘Models for’
citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: An agent-based account of models grounds the enactment of modeling in science classrooms
description: The article advances an agent-based account of models drawn from philosophy of science, in which models are understood relative to a cognitive agent's aims and intentions rather than solely as representations of phenomena in the world. The authors use this account to derive implications for enacting modeling in science classrooms, contrasting it with purely representational (semantic) views of models.
requirements: Understanding models requires attending to the agent or agents for whom the model is built and what they intend to do with it.
constraints: The account is presented as a philosophical position with implications for classrooms, not as an empirically tested model of learning.

target_learning_goals: Developing and using models as a scientific practice
examples: The authors discuss implications of this view for enacting modeling in science classrooms under the NGSS.

article_title: Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls
citation: Fuhrmann D., Casey C.S., Speekenbrink M., Blakemore S.-J. (2019). Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2019.100718
title: Design and time school social-exclusion interventions with age differences in cognitive vulnerability in mind
description: The article's stated practical implication is that responses to exclusion differ by age, so anti-bullying and social-exclusion work in schools should be designed and timed with those differences in mind. The authors write that their findings "underlin[e] the need to consider age differences in response to exclusion in the design and timing of social exclusion interventions in schools", because young adolescent girls' verbal working memory was affected by even a brief virtual exclusion while older groups' was not.
requirements: Interventions should be matched to the developmental stage of the students, since only young adolescents showed cognitive performance effects in this study
constraints: Evidence comes from a short virtual exclusion simulation with female participants only; the authors note real-life exclusion is repeated and more personal, and effects on males are unknown

mid-adolescents and adults as comparison groups
target_learning_goals: protecting working-memory-dependent academic performance from the effects of peer exclusion
examples: In the experiment, young adolescents (N=36) showed reduced n-back accuracy after exclusion while mid-adolescents and adults did not, and all groups completed the tasks individually in schools or the lab

article_title: Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities.
citation: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x
title: Design pedagogical agents with an equilibrium of utility and usability before investing in aesthetic elements
description: Drawing on interaction design, the article argues that for a pedagogical agent to be perceived as useful, "the design of the agent must embrace an equilibrium of utility and usability." Utility is the array of functionalities satisfying pedagogical requirements, and usability is the effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction with which learners accomplish tasks. Only once this balance is achieved can designers focus on aesthetic elements of the character to potentially enhance the learning experience.
requirements: Functionalities that satisfy the outlined pedagogical requirements and enable learners to accomplish their learning goals
constraints: A usable agent without needed learning support is worthless; a support-rich agent that is difficult to use leads to dissatisfied learners
target_learners: learners interacting with pedagogical agents in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: accomplishing learning goals through agent-supported tasks
examples: The article cites Mahmood and Ferneley's finding that quality of interaction was perceived as more important than visual design, and calls for further research on these properties with respect to the actual user experience.

citation: Price, Jodi; Hertzog, Christopher; Dunlosky, John. (2010). Self-Regulated Learning in Younger and Older Adults: Does Aging Affect Metacognitive Control? Neuropsychology, development, and cognition. Section B, Aging, neuropsychology and cognition. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825580903287941
title: Agenda-based regulation (ABR) account of older adults' self-regulated study
description: The agenda-based regulation model holds that item selection should be interpreted with respect to the task goals and agendas learners set, rather than item difficulty alone. The article uses it to explain why older adults avoided difficult items even when those items carried high point values: "older adults may also select and allocate study time based more on an agenda (e.g., avoid more difficult items regardless of their point value or experimenter-determined goals) than on item difficulty". It complements the region of proximal learning model, which both age groups' easy-to-difficult selection order otherwise supported.
requirements: Learners must set or be given task goals and agendas that can be compared against item difficulty and value when interpreting selection behavior
constraints: The article presents ABR as an interpretive account of these two experiments' findings, citing Ariel et al. (in press) for the model's original demonstration with younger adults
target_learners: younger and older adult learners studying paired-associate vocabulary
target_learning_goals: metacognitive control of item selection and study time allocation during self-regulated learning
examples: In Experiment 2, older adults' selections tended to favor easier items regardless of point value even when difficult items were worth the most points

article_title: Helping others use social media: age stereotypes when estimating learner’s success
citation: Harvey J. GINSBURG, Rebecca CAMERON, Roque V. MENDEZ & Michael WESTHOFF. (2016). Helping others use social media: age stereotypes when estimating learner's success. Psychology, Society, & Education, 8(1), 1-12. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1123456
title: Age stereotyping among young SNS users when estimating older learners' success
description: The article proposes that young social media users' lower success estimates for older learners reflect age stereotyping rather than actual learner ability. It argues that because older adults "may generally have more difficulty mastering nuances of social media", younger users may become "less likely to offer assistance", and that such stereotyping "would apply to increasing numbers of older SNS users regardless of their experience levels and proficiencies". The study's declining success estimates with learner age are presented as evidence consistent with this account.

constraints: The article frames this as possible stereotyping inferred from hypothetical scenarios; participants' attributions about the hypothetical friends or relatives were not identified

target_learning_goals: informal helping and teaching of social networking skills to older adult learners

description: A simulation-based learning environment in which a learner takes the role of an internist collaborating with an agent-based radiologist to diagnose fictitious patient cases with fever. Learners fill out request forms for radiological examinations, and only when they share evidence and hypotheses appropriately for their request do they receive the radiologist's findings. It operationalizes individual agency in terms of three relational directions: "Toward the self: regulating one's thoughts, emotions, and motivation to sustain engagement in the learning process", "Through others", and "Toward groups". citation: Keller, M. M., Yanagida, T., Lüdtke, O., & Goetz, T. (2025). How Similar Are Students' Aggregated State Emotions to Their Self-Reported Trait Emotions? title: Aggregation of momentary emotional states as a measurement route to trait emotions (Epstein's resolution of the person-situation debate)
description: This framework holds that emotional traits are stable dispositions that can be inferred by repeatedly measuring momentary emotional states and aggregating them per person, resolving the person-situation debate methodologically. The article explains that Epstein "recommends collecting momentary responses from a wide array of situations and time points to identify correlations with stable traits", so that common variance in repeated states captures a person-specific, trait-like component. The study applies this by aggregating experience-sampling state emotions over ten school days per year and comparing the aggregates to one-time trait self-reports on convergence, mean levels, stability, and predictive validity.
requirements: Repeated state assessments across multiple situations and time points (the study used ten consecutive school days of experience sampling per wave)
constraints: Traits here are conceived narrowly as classroom/domain-specific dispositions rather than lifelong dispositions; trait consistency across situations and stability over time cannot be assumed to be absolute

target_learning_goals: measuring students' domain-specific academic emotions (enjoyment, anger, pride, anxiety, shame, boredom) in German, English, French, and mathematics
examples: Students activated iPod Touch devices at the start of German, English, French, and mathematics lessons and reported momentary emotions when randomly signaled 10-35 min after activation, once per year across three school years

article_title: Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age?
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Generative Learning: Which Strategies for What Age? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09571-9
title: Match the amount of instructional support in generative learning activities to learners' age, giving younger learners more structure
description: The review concludes that generative learning strategies must be implemented with age-appropriate support: "younger learners generally need more support than older learners", and "a suboptimal implementation of the technique for a particular age group can render it ineffective". Support can take the form of pre-structured materials, such as high-coherence concept maps or fill-in maps, or prompts to compare generated products with provided ones. Without such scaffolding, younger children may produce poor-quality generative products and gain nothing.

secondary-school students

Sixth-graders' drawing benefit was enhanced when prompted to compare their drawing with a provided illustration

citation: Garvin Brod, Natalia Kucirkova, Joshua Shepherd, Dietsje Jolles, Inge Molenaar. (2023). Agency in Educational Technology: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Implications for Learning Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09749-x
title: Agency personalization loop: adaptive assignment of agency levels based on a student model and learning progress
description: The agency personalization loop is a three-step conceptualization for how personalized EdTech can adaptively assign levels of agency to learners. The loop lets agency "vary both between different learners and within a particular learner over time," balancing free choice against assigned optimal content.

The loop is deliberately generic and assumed applicable to various ways control can be shared between students and EdTech

Long and Aleven's shared control over problem selection in intelligent tutoring systems

article_title: Teachers’ immigration attitudes and students’ performance
citation: Anatolia Batruch, Nicolas Sommet, Eva G.T. Green. (2026). Teachers' immigration attitudes and students' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102303
title: Aggregated teachers' explicit immigration attitudes as an exogenous institutional indicator of school diversity climate (normative climate / structural bias account)
description: The article proposes measuring school diversity climates through teachers' immigration attitudes aggregated at the school level, rather than through students' perceptions. It argues this captures "exclusionary versus inclusionary 'normative climates'" and systemic or structural bias, because aggregation reflects "the prevalence of teachers' biases within schools but also the broader institutional norms that foster or legitimize them." The account holds that biases are embedded in institutional climates that shape outcomes for marginalized students, and that collective teacher attitudes act as social environmental cues of socioecological inclusion.

secondary school students

academic integration of immigrant students

article_title: An experimental critique of the Binet-Simon scale.
citation: Carl C. Brigham. (1914). An Experimental Critique of the Binet-Simon Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Classify Binet-Simon results by the difference between mental and chronological age, computed in tenths of a year
description: The article proposes a standardized method of classifying Binet-Simon results: calculate chronological age in tenths or fifths of a year, place the mental age in tenths or fifths giving credit for every test passed above the basal age, and classify by the difference between the two. The writer "would therefore suggest the following as the standardized method of classifying the results obtained from the Binet-Simon tests." This method avoids the double smoothing error that afflicts classifying first by chronological and then by mental age.
requirements: Calculate the chronological age in tenths or fifths of a year and the mental age in tenths or fifths, giving credit for every test passed above the basal age, then classify by years or half-years according to the amount of analysis the data will stand
constraints: Classification by age difference remains liable to one source of error — smoothing the figures to years or half-years
target_learners: school children in the first six grades assessed with the Binet-Simon scale
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and grading of intelligence and individual differences
examples: In this study the chronological ages were calculated in tenths of a year, and the age difference computed in tenths, applied to the 294 cases in the regular grades of the Princeton Model School.

title: Design conversational agents as teacher-configurable tools, not teacher replacements
description: The authors argue the agent "should not be designed as teacher replacement, but should serve as an intelligent tool enhancing the impact of the collaboration strategies employed by the teacher, who always remains responsible for the orchestration and scaffolding of the educational activity." This 'teacher-as-activity-designer' perspective motivates teacher-led configuration of domain models and intervention rules, aiming for broader teacher acceptance and reusability across domains.

article_title: Disparities in Students’ Propensity to Consent to Learning Analytics
citation: Warren Li, Kaiwen Sun, Florian Schaub, Christopher Brooks. (2022). Disparities in Students' Propensity to Consent to Learning Analytics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 32:564–608. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00254-2
title: Providing students agency over learning analytics consent is necessary but insufficient; institutions and instructors must build trust and transparency to prevent biased data collection
description: The article argues that offering students a consent choice alone will not produce representative participation, because subpopulations differ in trust and comfort. Students' "comments corroborate these findings and suggest that agency alone is insufficient; institutional leaders and instructors also play a large role in alleviating the issue of bias." The authors suggest instructors can bolster comfort "by being more transparent regarding who data is used and who has access to it."
requirements: Consent mechanisms must be paired with institutional and instructor actions that build student trust in how data is used and who has access to it.
constraints: The study was conducted at a single institution (University of Michigan) with a predominantly White, higher-socioeconomic-status student body, and used a hypothetical broad consent prompt rather than a live system.
target_learners: University students
target_learning_goals: Equitable participation in learning analytics data collection and unbiased predictive modeling of student outcomes
examples: The study sent an email-based one-question consent prompt to 4,000 stratified students and found Black students underrepresented (−40%) and White students overrepresented (31%) among respondents despite stratified recruitment.
key_sources: Warren Li, Kaiwen Sun, Florian Schaub, Christopher Brooks. (2022). Disparities in Students' Propensity to Consent to Learning Analytics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 32:564–608. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00254-2

title: Agent-based architecture for a collaborative case study system
description: LeCS is described as having an agent-based architecture in which software agents accomplish the system's support functions. The article announces a general description of LeCS covering "its user interface, implementation, and agent-based architecture," and states that the system "accomplishes functions regarding the learning process that together give real-time support to the distant learners." article_title: A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning
citation: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8
title: Teachable agent questioning system with five question categories
description: The agent asks the tutor situation-specific multiple-choice questions at the moment a card is chosen but before the computation is executed, to encourage mental calculation and reasoning. Questions are organized into five categories: game idea, graphical model, scoring, basic strategic thinking, and advanced strategic thinking. Question difficulty follows the agent's knowledge level, aligned with Vygotskij's zone of proximal development. Questions are posed every 3rd turn on average, about three questions per game.
requirements: Multiple-choice format with a don't-know option
Important questions are checked several times with different surface formulations
Progression requires 75% of previous questions answered satisfactorily
constraints: Questions are text-based and appear in a dialogue window
The youngest children are not good at writing, motivating the multiple-choice format
target_learners: primary school students grades 1-6
target_learning_goals: self-explanation
transfer of tacit game knowledge to articulated language
mathematical reasoning
examples: A question template compares two choices with respect to points, asking whether one card is better than another given the current game state

article_title: Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners’ Willingness to Communicate
citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: Design conversational agents for L2 learners to resolve communication pitfalls on the learner's behalf rather than leaving repair to the learner
description: Because L2 communication breakdowns occur more often than in L1 and too much difficulty may cause learners to abort their attempts, the article argues that an agent intended to increase WTC should itself handle conversational trouble. By enabling the ECA to use communication strategies, the authors aim 'to enhance its own strategic competence to release learners from the challenging and WTC-inhibiting burden of resolving communication pitfalls by themselves', hypothesizing that learners who can rely on a supportive agent develop a sense of security that increases confidence.
requirements: The agent needs a repertoire of communication strategies (e.g., repetition, simplification, code-switching) triggered by detected conversation states
constraints: The article notes that for learners with low WTC, mastering such strategies themselves does not guarantee they will use them when facing trouble
target_learners: L2 learners, especially those at lower proficiency levels who experience difficulty communicating in the target language
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate and confidence in L2 conversation
examples: In the dialogue excerpt of Fig. 3, successive agent interventions using AB and CS helped the learner gradually overcome an initial breakdown and finally produce the answer 'non-smoking please'

article_title: Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs
citation: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6
title: Adapt the dynamic support strategy to the contextual needs of different student populations (agile support)
description: Agile support for collaborative learning means adapting the facilitation strategy taken by the support technology to the specific contextual needs of different student populations, rather than applying the same context-sensitive rules for all groups. The article proposes that the choice of facilitation strategy can be adapted in response to an automated assessment of interaction patterns indicating whether a successful intervention is occurring. This principle is motivated by the finding that strategy effectiveness rankings differ across student populations and learning tasks.
requirements: An automated measure indicating the relative success of alternative intervention strategies within contexts
Insights into the contextual pre-conditions for the success of specific facilitation strategies
constraints: The article explicitly states it is not claiming to already have this agile form of support, only to provide the initial empirical foundation for developing such an approach
target_learners: urban public high school students
selective private university students
target_learning_goals: maximizing learning gains from collaborative discussion across diverse populations
examples: The article proposes adapting strategy choice in response to whether the characteristic pattern indicating a successful intervention is present in the ongoing collaboration

article_title: Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach

title: Capstone project with agile methodology funnelling all course tasks into one digital innovation artefact
description: An instructional element added after iteration 1 in which "a new principle was added to allow all tasks to be funnelled into a comprehensive capstone project that applies agile methods". Students work in teams with industry partners to design and implement a working digital innovation such as a mobile application or website, using open-source software. "The application of Agile allows changes to group formation, regular feedback and the assessment of the overall process and not merely the end solution."

Assessments measuring outcomes per week so teams can make improvements
constraints: Interpersonal issues in teams and requirement limitations with industry partners could not be pre-empted

target_learning_goals: Implementing a working digital innovation in a business
Collaboration and project management

article_title: The critical, relational practice of instructional design in higher education: an emerging model of change agency
citation: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007).
title: Agentic model of instructional design: four types of agency with intentional and operational dimensions
description: The article proposes a "complex and reflexive" agentic model of instructional design in which designers act as moral, political agents of change. Narrative data from twenty designers at six Canadian universities revealed four types of agency that "appeared to fit into four categories: interpersonal, professional, institutional and societal." The model carries intentional dimensions (values, principles) and operational dimensions (concrete actions), and designers move in and out of a zone of moral coherence across projects.
requirements: Agency types must be understood as grounded in designers' narratives of practice rather than frequency counts
constraints: The categories were not mutually exclusive, nor equally represented in the data
The model is explicitly tentative and emerging
target_learners: instructional designers in higher education
faculty clients of instructional designers
target_learning_goals: professional identity development
change agency in instructional design practice
examples: The model was developed from post hoc thematic analysis of research conversations, focus groups and story circles using Atlas Ti

article_title: Academic Competencies in Academic Global Surgery: A Scoping Review.
citation: Zolo Yvan, Mulwafu Wakisa, David Dalle Ulrich, Maswime Salome. (2026). Academic Competencies in Academic Global Surgery: A Scoping Review. ANZ Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1111/ans.70384
title: An 11-cluster competency framework for academic global surgery education
description: The review developed a competency framework by organizing thematic clusters from identified academic global surgery programs. It consists of 11 clusters: Surgical Systems and Health Systems Science; Leadership and Management; Research and Scientific Inquiry; Clinical and Technical Excellence; Policy, Advocacy and Diplomacy; Health Equity and Social Determinants; Education and Mentorship; Ethics, Cultural Competency and Professionalism; Innovation and Implementation Science; Communication and Interdisciplinary Collaboration; and Emergency and Humanitarian Surgery. Each cluster includes related sub-competencies and representative examples drawn from program content, with relative emphasis ranging from "Very Common" to "Less Common".
requirements: Derived from a scoping review of peer-reviewed studies and grey literature describing academic global surgery programs between 2000 and 2024.
constraints: The framework reflects the programs captured in this review; the authors note no universally accepted core competency framework currently guides these programs.
target_learners: Health professionals in academic global surgery training programs
target_learning_goals: Surgical systems strengthening, leadership, research, health equity, and related competencies in global surgery

article_title: If It's about Me, Why Do It without Me? Genuine Student Engagement in School Cyberbullying Education
citation: Donna Cross, Leanne Lester, Amy Barnes, Patricia Cardoso and Kate Hadwen. (2015). If it’s about me, why do it without me? Genuine student engagement in school cyberbullying education. International Journal of Emotional Education, 7(1), 35-51. www.um.edu.mt/cres/ijee
title: Agency, belonging and competence as the three assets enhanced by authentic student participation in school decision-making
description: The article adopts Mitra's (2004) framework that student involvement in school decision-making enhances three key assets: agency (expressing opinions, perceiving oneself as a change maker, developing leadership skills), belonging (caring relationships with adults and attachment to school), and competence (assessing the school environment and building problem-solving, public speaking and social skills). The CFSP applies this framework to cyberbullying prevention, and the authors conclude the data suggest the training and support "contributed positively to their growing sense of agency, belonging and competence". It organises the paper's discussion sections and its research questions.
requirements: Students must be given authentic opportunities to contribute to school decision-making, with adults in supportive rather than dominating roles.
constraints: The article notes that when adults do not give students agency to make and implement decisions, roles largely revert to teachers dominating students' decision-making (citing Mitra, 2004).
target_learners: secondary school students (grade 8-10 adolescents)
target_learning_goals: social and emotional skills, leadership skills, and cyberbullying prevention knowledge
examples: CFSP cyber leaders planned and led whole-school activities each school term, with most self-assessing at Level 7 on Hart's ladder, initiating and directing their own ideas with adults in advisory roles.

citation: Thomas N. Janicki, Judith Gebauer, Ulku Yaylacicegi. (2011). Impact of Pre-Grading / Resubmission of Projects on Test Grades in an Introductory Computer Literacy Course. Information Systems Education Journal 9(2). http://www.aitp-edsig.org
title: Adaptive Grading/Learning System (AGLS), a custom-built automated grader with rapid personalized feedback, shared assignment libraries, and plagiarism detection

It "consists of modules that provide automated grading of Microsoft Excel 2007 and Access 2007 assignments with personalized and rapid feedback, assignment libraries that can be shared among participating instructors, and plagiarism detection". It also lets instructors increase exercise complexity without much additional effort, and it supports pre-grading rounds in which comments point to what needs correction rather than giving solutions.

target_learning_goals: spreadsheet and database skills (Excel 2007, Access 2007)

article_title: [Agency: occupational therapists' perspectives on their sense of competence and their skills following training].
citation: Carrier Annie, Éthier Alexandra, Beaudoin Michaël, Hudon Anne, Bédard Denis, Jasmin Emmanuelle, Lavoie-Trudeau Étienne, Verville France. (2024). Agency: occupational therapists’ perspectives on their sense of competence and their skills following training. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.78346
title: Agency (agentivité) as the capacity to act according to what is considered worthwhile, exercisable individually or collectively and developable
description: The article frames agency (agentivité) as occupational therapists' power to act, needed to tackle systemic injustices affecting people in vulnerable situations. It is "définie comme la capacité d’agir en fonction de ce qui est considéré comme valable", can be exercised individually or collectively, and can be developed in a person. Agency requires both process-freedom and the feeling of being able to act, called sense of competence, which motivational dynamics theory positions as essential for engagement and perseverance.
requirements: Both freedom of process and realization, and a sense of competence, are needed for agency
constraints: The article addresses agency specifically in the context of occupational therapists acting as change agents against systemic injustices
target_learners: practising occupational therapists
occupational therapy students
target_learning_goals: developing agency and sense of competence to act as a change agent
examples: The article links a stronger sense of competence to more frequent mobilization of competencies, perseverance facing obstacles, and increased motivation to act
